interviewQuestions.question: How would you prevent two users from booking the same seat at the same time?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start by naming the actual bug: a check-then-act read of seat status followed by a separate write leaves a race window where two requests can both pass the check. So the fix is to fold the check into the write itself — an atomic conditional update like `UPDATE seats SET state='HELD' WHERE seat_id=? AND state='AVAILABLE'` — and look at rows-affected instead of doing a prior read.

I'd walk through why an in-process lock (`synchronized` on a `Show` object) isn't enough once there's more than one app server — each server's lock only protects its own process, so the race just moves to the database, which is where the real fix has to live.

I'd close by covering holds: every hold needs a server-enforced TTL, checked lazily on next access, so abandoned checkouts don't lock out inventory forever.

**Testing:** whether you can name the exact race condition and push the fix down to an atomic database operation, rather than answering "use a lock" without specifics.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Preventing concurrent double-booking

interviewQuestions.question: How would you handle a flash sale for a blockbuster's opening show?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame this as: the general design already works for 99% of shows — the flash sale only breaks it because a handful of the best seats suddenly see extreme contention from thousands of requests in seconds. So I'd scope the fix to that specific hotspot rather than redesigning the whole system.

Concretely: a virtual waiting room or rate limiter in front of checkout smooths the request burst; shortening the hold TTL during the sale window frees contested seats faster; and for the specific hot seats, I'd consider a lightweight in-memory queue per seat instead of raw database contention, since retrying a database write thousands of times per second on the same row wastes capacity.

I'd also flag that this is a temporary, predictable spike — over-engineering the steady-state design for it is the wrong trade.

**Testing:** whether you can scale the one hot path precisely instead of proposing a blanket, always-on solution.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Scaling for a blockbuster opening

interviewQuestions.question: Why model Seat with its own lifecycle instead of a boolean 'isBooked' flag on Show?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd point out that a boolean can only say booked or not — it can't represent the state that makes concurrent checkout safe in the first place: HELD, where a seat is neither free nor confirmed, just reserved for one user's checkout window. Collapsing HELD into "booked" would let a second user see the seat as available the instant the first person starts checkout, defeating the whole hold mechanism; collapsing it into "available" would let two holds stack on the same seat.

So `Seat` carries an explicit status — AVAILABLE, HELD, BOOKED — plus a `holdExpiresAt` timestamp for the HELD state, and every transition is a guarded, atomic operation (AVAILABLE to HELD, HELD to BOOKED on payment success, HELD back to AVAILABLE on payment failure or TTL expiry). This also makes the release-on-expiry logic clean: a scheduled sweep or lazy check-on-access just looks for seats past their `holdExpiresAt` and flips them back, without needing to reason about a boolean's history.

I'd close by noting this is a smaller version of the same lesson as the Show's own state machine — any entity with a real "reserved but not yet final" state needs more than two values to be modeled honestly.

**Testing:** whether you recognize a boolean can't represent an in-between reserved state, and reach for an explicit status instead of bolting on more flags.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why Seat needs a lifecycle

interviewQuestions.question: The interviewer now adds a policy allowing cancellation up to 30 minutes before showtime with a partial refund — what changes?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame this as adding one new legal transition rather than reworking the booking flow: `Booking` gains a CANCELLED terminal state reachable from CONFIRMED, guarded by a check against `show.startTime - now() >= 30 minutes` at the moment cancellation is requested, not at booking time, since the 30-minute window is relative to a clock that keeps moving.

The seat side effect matters as much as the booking side: cancelling has to flip the `Seat` back to AVAILABLE so it re-enters inventory for other buyers, and I'd make that seat-release and the booking-status change part of one transaction — a booking that shows CANCELLED while its seat still shows BOOKED is a worse bug than the double-booking this whole design was built to prevent.

For the partial refund, I'd route the actual money movement through a `PaymentService.refund(amount)` call rather than computing it inline in `Booking`, since refund percentage (say, 80% inside the window) is a business rule that's likely to change independently of the booking model — I'd model it as its own small `RefundPolicy` so a future "free cancellation for premium members" rule doesn't require touching `Booking` again.

**Testing:** whether you can add a real product requirement as a contained extension — new transition, existing seat-release mechanism reused, refund logic isolated — rather than treating it as a from-scratch feature.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Adding cancellation with partial refund
